newsitem.title: ITALY: Italian government showdown looms over Albania.
newsitem.headline: Italian government showdown looms over Albania.

text.p: Foreign Minister Lamberto Dini called on Saturday for a showdown in Italy's shaky coalition to determine whether the government could survive a rift over plans to send 2,000 troops to Albania.
"Things can't go on like this," Dini, who leads the centrist Italian Renewal party, told reporters.
"I hope it will be possible to put things back together within the (parliamentary) majority but we have got to clear matters up," he said. "I believe we have to do it fast."

Prime Minister Romano Prodi, in office since May last year, is battling opposition within his fractious alliance to sending soldiers into Albania at the head of the first Italian-led multinational force in post-war history.
Objections have come from the Greens, who are part of Prodi's centre-left government, and the parliamentary party he relies upon to survive, the hard-left Communist Refoundation.

The U.N.-authorised force of some 6,000 men from up to eight nations is due to deploy in the week starting April 14 to assist an international relief effort to the Balkan state, rocked by weeks of armed anarchy.

Political sources said Prodi had called a coalition summit for Monday to try to restore unity ahead of formal votes on the mission in the Senate (upper house) and the Chamber of Deputies (lower house) next Tuesday and Wednesday.
Prodi's victory in parliament is not in doubt since he has the backing of the main opposition centre-right bloc.

But hard-left resistance has shaken Prodi's unsteady coalition to the core, raised doubts about the reaction if the force runs into trouble and, say Italian commentators, dented Italy's international credibility.
"Italy is making a terrible mess of the first international crisis it has to manage alone," commentator Gianni Riotta wrote in Corriere della Sera newspaper.

Refoundation leader Fausto Bertinotti insists that he does not intend to bring down the government over Albania, but there has been little sign that his party will drop its plans to vote 'no' to the force rather than abstain or back it.
"Summit or no summit, that doesn't change our opinion," Refoundation foreign affairs spokesman Ramon Mantovani said.
Opposition politicians say they believe Prodi's coalition will ultimately overcome the fracas and stay in office.
But coalition parties are now talking openly of either moving to an early election or ditching Refoundation and trying to form a minority government unless Bertinotti backs down.
They are already frustrated by Refoundation's refusal to countenance welfare spending cuts in Prodi's do-or-die drive to put Italy on course to join Europe's planned single currency.
Italian leadership of the Albania force had already been complicated by the fatal sinking of a packed refugee vessel off Italy on March 28 in a collision with an Italian navy corvette.
One of Bertinotti's arguments against the force is that anti-Italian passions raised by the affair will expose soldiers to unacceptable risks from lawless gunmen.

The Albanian state news agency ATA said on Saturday that Prime Minister Bashkim Fino had reassured Dini in a telephone call that "Italian troops will have maximum security and complete support from the... government and public opinion".

"The Prime Minister said that he was attentively following the debate in the Italian parliament on the problems and gave assurances that the concern expressed by some forces in (Italy's) parliamentary majority is exaggerated," ATA said.
